sources.title: IMF DataMapper - GDP, current prices (NGDPD), India
sources.snippet: IMF DataMapper (WEO series NGDPD) projects India's nominal GDP at US$3.909T (2025), US$4.060T (2026), US$4.521T (2027), US$4.996T (2028), US$5.542T (2029), US$6.130T (2030), US$6.744T (2031). Implied crossing years: $5T in 2029, $6T in 2030; $7T is NOT reached within the IMF horizon (ends 2031 at $6.74T). | 2025: 3,908.964; 2026: 4,060.207; 2027: 4,521.197; 2028: 4,995.623; 2029: 5,542.035; 2030: 6,129.559; 2031: 6,744.026 (US$ billions, calendar-year basis per IMF) | tier 1, HIGH confidence

sources.title: Weak rupee delays India's $5 trillion economy goal to 2029
sources.snippet: IMF Oct-2026 revision cut India's 2028 nominal GDP to $4.996T from ~$5.1T six months earlier, pushing $5T to 2029; driver is exchange-rate assumption (INR ~95.5/USD in 2028 vs 93.3 in April projection), not weaker rupee-terms growth. | 2028: $4.996T (prev ~$5.1T); INR 95.5/USD assumed for 2028 | tier 3, MEDIUM confidence

sources.title: IMF thinks India's $5 trn economy goal will take one more year. Here's what changed
sources.snippet: IMF consultation report released 26 Nov 2025 projected India to hit $5T in FY29, a year later than previously projected; FY28 at $4.96T. | FY28: $4.96T; $5T in FY29 | tier 2, MEDIUM confidence

sources.title: Indian economy poised to hit $7.3 trillion by 2030: Finance Ministry report ('The Indian Economy - A Review', Jan 2024)
sources.snippet: Finance Ministry review (led by CEA V. Anantha Nageswaran): 'India can aspire to become a USD 7 trillion economy in the next six to seven years (by 2030)'. Business Today headline frames it as $7.3T by 2030. Note: IMF Oct-2026 data put 2030 at $6.13T, so the $7T-by-2030 aspiration is now well above IMF baseline. | $7T by 2030 (aspirational) | tier 2, MEDIUM confidence

sources.title: India's Q4 GDP expands 7.8%, taking full-year growth to 7.7%: Govt data
sources.snippet: MoSPI Provisional Estimates (5 June 2026, new 2022-23 base series): 'Nominal GDP, or GDP at current prices, has been estimated to attain a level of Rs 346.36 lakh crore in 2025-26', growth 8.9%; real GDP growth 7.7% (vs 7.1% in 2024-25). | FY2025-26 nominal GDP Rs 346.36 lakh crore (+8.9%); real growth 7.7% | tier 2, MEDIUM confidence

sources.title: India set to become $6 trillion economy by 2030: Standard Chartered research
sources.snippet: Standard Chartered research projected India becoming a $6T economy by 2030. | $6T by 2030 | tier 3, LOW confidence

sources.title: Does Management Matter? Evidence from India
sources.snippet: Randomised management consulting in large Indian textile firms: published abstract reports 'adopting these management practices raised productivity by 17% in the first year'; treated firms opened more plants within three years. NBER WP (Jan 2011) version reported productivity +11% and annual profitability +about $230,000. | +17% productivity in first year (QJE); +11% productivity and ~+$230,000/yr profit per firm (NBER WP 16658) | tier 1, HIGH confidence

sources.title: Does Management Matter? Evidence from India (NBER WP 16658)
sources.snippet: 'A major reason is that the owners were severely time constrained, working an average of 68 hours per week already. There was also evidence of procrastination in that some owners would defer on taking quick decisions.' | Owners worked avg 68 hours/week | tier 1, HIGH confidence

sources.title: CEO Behavior and Firm Performance
sources.snippet: Diary data on 1,114 CEOs in six countries (Brazil, France, Germany, India, UK, US; 356 in India). Two types: 'Leaders focus on multi-function, high-level meetings, while managers focus on one-to-one meetings with core functions.' 'We estimate that 17% of sample CEOs are mismatched'; 'These inefficient assignments are more frequent in lower income countries (36% vs 5%). The productivity loss generated by the misallocation of CEOs to firms equals 13% of the labor productivity gap between high and low income countries.' Average CEO logged ~50 hours/week. CEO behaviour index significantly lower (more 'manager'-type) in Brazil and India. | 17% mismatched overall; 36% in low/middle-income (Brazil, India) vs 5% high-income; mismatch = up to 13% of cross-country labour-productivity gap | tier 1, HIGH confidence

sources.title: Managing the Family Firm: Evidence from CEOs at Work
sources.snippet: 'The comparison of 1,114 family and professional CEOs reveals that family CEOs work 9% fewer hours relative to professional CEOs. Hours worked are positively correlated with firm performance, and differences between family and non-family CEOs account for approximately 18% of the performance gap between family and non-family firms.' Sample includes 356 Indian CEOs. | Family CEOs -9% hours; explains ~18% of family vs non-family performance gap | tier 1, HIGH confidence

sources.title: Managerial capital at the top: evidence on CEOs time use and firm performance in India
sources.snippet: Average Indian CEO recorded ~39 work hours/week; 56% of time in in-person meetings; 12% e-meetings; 12% working alone; 6% plant visits; 7% travel. Production-related people take the largest share: about 9 hours/week, or 35%. Over three-quarters of firms owned by founders/family; 68% of CEOs belong to owning family. 'Firms' productivity is higher when CEOs work longer hours but not all CEOs' time is equally productive.' | 35% of CEO time on production-related interactions; 56% in meetings; 68% family CEOs | tier 1, LOW confidence

sources.title: The Life Cycle of Plants in India and Mexico
sources.snippet: 'In the U.S., the average 40 year old plant employs almost eight times as many workers as the typical plant five years or younger. In contrast, surviving Indian plants exhibit little growth in terms of either employment or output.' Mexican 40-year-old plants employ twice as many as new plants. Life-cycle differences 'could lower aggregate manufacturing productivity on the order of 25% in India and Mexico relative to the U.S.' | US ~8x employment growth age <5 to 40; India ~no growth; Mexico 2x; ~25% aggregate TFP loss | tier 1, HIGH confidence

sources.title: How CEOs Manage Time
sources.snippet: 27 CEOs (avg revenue $13.1B) tracked 24/7 for 13 weeks, 60,000 hours. 72% of work time in meetings (37 meetings/week); ~36% reactive mode 'handling unfolding issues'; 43% on activities furthering their agendas (range 14%-80%); 21% on strategy; 25% functional and business unit reviews; 25% developing people and relationships; 16% organisation/culture; 4% M&A; 11% routine duties; 75% of time scheduled in advance; 9.7 hours per weekday plus work on 79% of weekend days. | 72% meetings; 36% reactive; 43% agenda; 21% strategy; 25% functional/BU reviews | tier 1, HIGH confidence

sources.title: PwC India Family Business Survey 2016: Aligning with India's growth story
sources.snippet: PwC India Family Business Survey 2016: ~1/3 planned to pass business fully to next generation (down from 40% in 2014); nearly half planned to keep family ownership but bring in professional management; 69% wanted experienced non-family managers to professionalise. | 69% want non-family professional managers (India, 2016) | tier 1, LOW confidence

sources.title: The prevalence and co-occurrence of psychiatric conditions among entrepreneurs and their families
sources.snippet: 'Mental health differences directly or indirectly affected 72% of the entrepreneurs in this sample' (personal history 49%; family history among asymptomatic 23%). Sample: 242 entrepreneurs, 93 comparison participants (US convenience sample). Depression 30%, ADHD 29%, substance use 12%, bipolar 11%; 32% had two or more conditions. | 72% affected; 30% depression | tier 1, MEDIUM confidence

sources.title: Mental health crisis in startups: study finds 47.5% report low wellbeing
sources.snippet: 'State of Mind: The Startup Ecosystem' study: 823 retained responses; 47.5% of respondents recorded low wellbeing; founders 42.9% low wellbeing (employees 54.3% per search snippet). | 42.9% of founders low wellbeing | tier 3, LOW confidence

sources.title: Designing a Policy for Medium Enterprises
sources.snippet: 'The sector remains largely dominated by micro enterprises, which constitute 97% of the registered MSMEs, followed by Small Enterprises (2.7%) and medium enterprises (0.3%).' Medium enterprises 'contribute 40% of MSME export income'; 67,923 medium entities, 58% in manufacturing; FY2022-23 medium-enterprise exports US$50,562.1 million. | Medium = 0.3% of registered MSMEs (67,923 entities) but ~40% of MSME export income | tier 1, HIGH confidence

sources.title: Economic Survey 2018-19, Vol 1, Ch 3: Nourishing Dwarfs to become Giants: Reorienting policies for MSME Growth
sources.snippet: 'While dwarfs, i.e., firms with less than 100 workers despite being more than ten years old, account for more than half of all organized firms in manufacturing by number, their contribution to employment is only 14 per cent and to productivity is a mere 8 per cent. In contrast, large firms (more than 100 employees) account for three-quarters of such employment and close to 90 per cent of productivity despite accounting for about 15 per cent by number.' Body text: dwarfs' employment share 14.1%, NVA share 7.6%. | >50% of organised manufacturing firms are dwarfs; 14% employment; 8% productivity | tier 1, HIGH confidence

sources.title: The Missing "Missing Middle"
sources.snippet: Using microdata for India, Indonesia and Mexico: 'there is no "missing middle" in the sense of a bimodal distribution'; 'large firms, not small firms, have higher average products'; 'no economically meaningful bunching of firms near the notch points'. Implies the issue is a 'missing large/growth' problem rather than a regulatory notch. | Qualitative | tier 1, HIGH confidence

sources.title: Govt. Revises Investment and Turnover Criteria for Classifying Enterprises as MSMEs
sources.snippet: Revised MSME criteria notified via S.O. 1364(E) dated 21 Mar 2025, effective 1 Apr 2025. Medium: investment up to ₹125 Cr (was ₹50 Cr) and turnover up to ₹500 Cr (was ₹250 Cr). Small: ₹25 Cr / ₹100 Cr. Micro: ₹2.5 Cr / ₹10 Cr. Implication: 'medium enterprise' now covers ₹100–₹500 Cr turnover, i.e. the bottom half of Aroh's ICP band. | Medium = investment ≤ ₹125 Cr AND turnover ≤ ₹500 Cr (from 1 Apr 2025) | tier Tier 1 (government notification, via secondary reporting), HIGH confidence

sources.snippet: As of 31 Jul 2026, 9.16 crore MSMEs registered on Udyam + Udyam Assist; split 9,11,07,705 micro, 5,40,908 small and 41,722 medium (per Ministry reply reported by Kashmir Life). This SUPPORTS the source doc's 'roughly 42,000 registered medium enterprises' but the date should read 'as of 31 July 2026' (not October 2026) and the source should be the Ministry parliamentary reply rather than dashboard.msme.gov.in (dashboard could not be opened — TLS error). | 41,722 medium enterprises (as of 2026-07-31) | tier Tier 1 data via Tier 2/3 regional press, MEDIUM confidence

sources.snippet: NITI Aayog 'Designing a Policy for Medium Enterprises' (May 2025) is reported as ~0.3% of registered MSMEs being medium; Drishti IAS summarises this as ~69,300 medium units on Udyam (Feb 2025) out of 5.93 crore.
